name: LMR64010XMFX_NOPB
title: 1.6 MHz current-mode boost regulator with a 40 V, 1 A internal switch, SOT-23

source.revision: SNVS736B, September 2011, revised April 2013 (addendum pages dated 2025)

summary: The LMR64010 is a SIMPLE SWITCHER step-up regulator in a five-pin SOT-23. It drives a 40 V internal FET at a fixed 1.6 MHz under current-mode control with internal loop compensation; a resistor divider and a feed-forward capacitor set the output, up to 40 V. It runs from 2.7 V to 14 V, limits the switch at 1 A minimum cycle by cycle (1.5 A typical) and shuts down thermally; pulling SHDN low cuts supply current below 1 µA.
key_figures: 500 mΩ typ, 650 mΩ max at 100 mA

circuits.title: 5 V to 20 V boost
circuits.description: Steps a 5 V rail up to 20 V. With the internal switch closed, L1 charges from the input; when it opens, the inductor current flows through the Schottky D1 into the output capacitor C2. The divider R1 (205 kΩ) over R2 (13.3 kΩ) returns the output to FB, regulated at 1.23 V, and the 120 pF CF across R1 places the loop zero the part needs. R3 pulls SHDN up to the input so the regulator runs until SHDN is driven low. C1 is the input reservoir.

circuits.title: Basic application circuit (Figure 17)
circuits.description: The general boost arrangement the design equations refer to. R1 and R2 set VOUT through R1 = R2 × (VOUT / 1.23 - 1), with R2 near 13.3 kΩ; Cf across R1 is chosen for a zero near 8 kHz. L1 charges while SW is low and discharges through D1 into C2. R3 holds SHDN up at the input; C1 is the input reservoir.
notes: R1, R2 and Cf are set by equations (1) and (2).

circuits.title: Typical application, 5 V to 12 V boost (Figure 19)
circuits.description: Raises 5 V to 12 V. L1 charges through the internal switch and dumps into C2 through the MBR0520 Schottky D1 when the switch turns off. R1 (117 kΩ) and R2 (13.3 kΩ) feed a fraction of the output back to FB at 1.23 V; 220 pF CF across R1 adds the zero needed for loop stability. R3 keeps SHDN high from the input unless an outside signal pulls it low. C1 is the ceramic input reservoir.

operation.text: A clock at a fixed 1.6 MHz sets an S-R latch each cycle, turning the switch FET on. A 50 mΩ sense resistor in the FET's source turns its current into a voltage, which is added to a ramp and compared with the Gm error amplifier's output in the PWM comparator; when it crosses, the latch resets and the FET turns off. Because the Gm output follows the feedback, the comparator settles the peak FET current that keeps the output regulated.
Q1, Q2 and R3 to R6 make a bandgap reference. The loop drives the output until the currents in Q1 and Q2 match, which holds FB at the reference and so the output at FB times the divider ratio.

A current-limit comparator works on the same sense voltage and resets the flip-flop directly, whatever the PWM comparator is doing. The FET stays off for the rest of that cycle and turns on again at the next clock. The minimum limit is 1 A at duty cycles under 50 % and it falls at higher duty cycles (Figure 20).
Thermal shutdown protects the part alongside the cycle-by-cycle current limit; past its dissipation limit the output voltage is lowered to keep the junction temperature safe.

Inside: VIN feeds R5 and R6 to the collectors of Q1 and Q2 (Q2 ten times Q1); FB drives the base of Q1, a resistor joins the bases of Q1 and Q2, and R3 30 kΩ over R4 140 kΩ carry the emitter currents to ground. The Gm amplifier compares the two collectors; its output, with RC and CC to ground, feeds the PWM comparator's + input, whose - input is the sum of the ramp generator and the current-sense amplifier across the 0.05 Ω resistor. The PWM comparator, the current-limit comparator and thermal shutdown each reset the flip-flop; the oscillator sets it. Its Q output drives the gate of the N-channel switch through a driver. Pin 4 enters the shutdown circuitry; the switch drain is pin 1 and the sense resistor returns to pin 2.

Pulling SHDN low (below 0.50 V) turns the device off; above 1.5 V it runs. With shutdown unused, tie SHDN straight to VIN; with shutdown used, a pull-up of roughly 50 kΩ to 100 kΩ to VIN is needed. SHDN must never be left open. Its voltage must stay at or below VIN + 0.3 V.

Multilayer ceramics suit the part best for their low ESR and high resonant frequency. Use only X5R or X7R: Z5U and Y5F lose so much with temperature and bias that as little as 20 % of the rated value may remain. Consult the capacitor vendor's curves before choosing.

One ceramic of 4.7 µF to 10 µF is enough in most designs; outputs under 10 V need 10 µF. Tantalum parts may be added in parallel for line support and transient response. Ultra-low-ESR aluminium types such as Sanyo Oscon work but cost a lot; ordinary aluminium electrolytics ring and self-heat above 500 kHz and do not suit. Too much output ESR erodes phase margin and can make the loop unstable.

An input capacitor supplies the current pulse into the inductor at every switch turn-on, so it must have very low ESR: use a ceramic, 2.2 µF nominal or more. It also lowers ripple at VIN and the EMI sent back up the supply line.
Despite the internal compensation, Cf across R1 is required for stability: it adds a zero to the loop, and without it the loop can oscillate. Aim the zero at about 8 kHz using equation (1).

Use a Schottky. Switch voltage below 15 V: a 20 V part such as MBR0520. 15 V to 25 V: a 30 V part such as MBR0530. Above 25 V: a 40 V part such as MBR0540. The MBR05xx parts carry up to 0.5 A average; between 0.5 A and 1 A average a Toshiba CRS08 can be used.

Place every part as close to the device as possible; a four-layer board with inner ground planes is recommended. Keep the L1, D1, C2 path very short: stray trace inductance along D1 and C2 brings noise and ringing. Keep R1, R2 and CF near the FB pin so noise is not coupled onto the FB trace. With an inner ground plane, take vias straight down from pin 2 and from the negative ends of C1 and C2.

Suggested placement (Figure 16): U1 in the centre with C1 just below-right of it and L1 to the right, over a VIN copper area; D1 above U1 near pin 1 and C2 above-left, both on a VOUT area; R1 and CF to the left of U1 and R2, R3 below it. Vias to the ground plane sit at C2, at U1's ground pin and at C1.
R2 from FB to ground is suggested near 13.3 kΩ, which puts about 92 µA through the divider; R1 from the output to FB then follows from equation (2).

The highest duty cycle limits the largest output-to-input ratio the converter can reach in continuous mode. Equation (3) includes the switch and diode drops; inductor winding loss, switching loss and capacitor heating push the measured duty cycle a little higher, and 1 - efficiency × VIN / VOUT estimates it better.

A larger inductor gives less ripple current and so usually less output ripple, and because the switch is limited on its peak current, more load power is available; too little inductance can cap the load current. Continuous mode, in which the inductor current never reaches zero during a cycle, generally gives better load regulation and lower ripple; every boost turns discontinuous at light enough load, but a larger inductor holds continuous mode down to a lower load.

For 5 V to 12 V with 10 µH (VDIODE and VSW taken as 0.5 V): the period is about 0.625 µs, duty cycle 62.5 %, on-time 0.390 µs and off-time 0.235 µs. About 4.5 V sits across the inductor while the switch is on, giving 0.45 A/µs and 0.176 A of ripple; the converter goes discontinuous below about 33 mA of load (Figure 18). The same circuit delivers 330 mA typical (Figure 19).

VSW in the equations depends on load: estimate it as the FET on-resistance times the average inductor current. The FET gate is clamped internally at 5 V, so on-resistance rises at VIN below 5 V, where gate drive is lower (Figure 8).
Equation (10) gives an estimate; Figure 21 gives bench-measured maximum load current for a typical device at output voltages of 15 V to 40 V against input voltage.

At high duty cycles the long on-time means dissipation in the FET switch, rather than the current limit, can set the maximum output current. Conduction loss is DC × IIND(AVE)² × RDSON; allow some derating for switching losses as well.

Where load current is small, the smallest inductor can be used and the converter left in discontinuous mode, provided the switch current peak stays below the 1 A limit during the longest on-time. Take the lowest frequency, 1.15 MHz (0.870 µs period). For 5 V to 12 V with VSW 0.2 V and VDIODE 0.3 V the duty cycle is 60.3 % and the on-time at most 0.524 µs; with 4.8 V across the inductor the current rises from zero to under 1 A, then falls to zero in 0.346 µs (Figure 22). The minimum is 2.5 µH, so 2.7 µH serves if it holds its value up to 1 A.
Choose a continuous current rating that keeps the core out of saturation at the peak current, a core type with low switching (core) loss, and allow for winding loss in the current rating.
